t.1.14.1: Śaunaka said: O Sauti, tell us once again, in full detail, this very story of the wise and virtuous Āstīka, for our desire to hear it is great indeed.
t.1.14.2: Sweetly is this spoken by you, gentle one, in smooth syllables and words; we are greatly delighted, dear son, for you speak this like a father.
t.1.14.3: For your father was ever devoted to our service; your father recounted this according to the tale, so you too tell it in the same way.
t.1.14.4: The Sūta said: I shall tell you this life-giving tale of Āstīka, just as it was heard by me from the presence of my father as he narrated it.
t.1.14.6: Those two, Kadrū and Vinatā, were the wives of Kaśyapa. Pleased, their husband Kaśyapa, equal to Prajāpati, filled with supreme joy, granted a boon to his two lawful wives.
t.1.14.5: Long ago, O brahmin, in the age of the gods, in the time of the auspicious son of Prajāpati, there lived two sisters, endowed with beauty, wondrous and sinless.
t.1.14.7: Upon hearing from Kaśyapa of the supreme granting of the boons, those two excellent women, out of joy, attained a delight beyond compare.
t.1.14.8: Kadrū chose as her sons a thousand serpents of equal splendor; Vinatā chose two sons surpassing the sons of Kadrū in strength, two sons superior in vigor, in splendor, and in valor.
t.1.14.10: Vinatā, having obtained two sons surpassing in valor, felt her purpose fulfilled, and so did Kadrū, having obtained a thousand sons of equal splendor.
t.1.14.9: To her the husband granted the boon she had wished for, a son and a half, and Vinatā then said to Kaśyapa, “So be it.”
t.1.14.11: Having said, "The two embryos must be borne with care," the great ascetic Kaśyapa entered the forest, while his two wives were thrilled with joy at the boon.
t.1.14.13: The delighted attendants placed the eggs of those two in moist, warm vessels, and there they kept them for five hundred years.
t.1.14.12: After a long time, O best of Brahmins, Kadrū brought forth ten hundreds of eggs, and Vinatā then brought forth two eggs.
t.1.14.14: Then, when five hundred years had passed, the sons of Kadrū came forth; but from the two eggs of Vinatā no pair of offspring was seen.
t.1.14.15: Then the goddess Vinatā, that poor ascetic woman, longing for a son and ashamed, broke open the egg, and there she saw her son.
t.1.14.17: Mother, since I have been made thus by you, overcome by greed, and am today incomplete in body, you shall therefore become a slave.
t.1.14.16: He was endowed with the upper half of his body, while the other half did not appear; and that son, filled with anger, cursed her, so the tradition says.
t.1.14.18: For five hundred years you shall be the slave of her with whom you compete; and this son, mother, will free you from slavery.
t.1.14.21: Having thus cursed Vinatā, her son Aruṇa then went into the sky, and he is always seen, O brahmin, at the time of dawn.
t.1.14.19: If you, mother, do not, by breaking his egg as you did with me, make this pitiable one too bodiless or deformed...
t.1.14.22: Garuḍa too, the destroyer of serpents, was born in due time. As soon as he was born, he left Vinatā and entered the sky.
t.1.14.20: If you desire surpassing strength, you must wait with steadfastness for the time of its birth, which will come after five hundred years.
t.1.14.23: O tiger among the Bhṛgus, he was about to take for himself the food that the Creator had ordained for him, for he was hungry and longing to eat.
